column76: I tried this thinking about my granddad who had a stroke last year. The 9-to-5 workday routine is brilliant because it feels like actual productive work instead of therapy, which keeps morale up.
column77: Everything ran smoothly, though having the keyboard shortcuts written somewhere on the screen would make it easier to help someone through a session.
column78: Let users pick different paint colors like blue or green, or pick rooms like a porch or kitchen. It'd make finishing each wall feel a lot more personal and fun.
column79: Really appreciate that it treats older adults with dignity. No talking down or babyish graphics, which my granddad would have hated.
column87: Maybe add a quick tip during setup about chair armrest clearance so people don't accidentally bump their elbow while seated.

column76: The Hindi voice prompts and the painter theme were great. My mother gets flustered by English apps, so hearing clear instructions in Hindi made it feel welcoming and normal.
column77: Keeping the hand still in the air for the pointer was a bit tiring while sitting down. Switching to the voice commands was way easier.
column78: A quick 3-second audio countdown in Hindi before the paint stroke starts so you have time to get your arm in position.
column79: Really thoughtful design for older relatives who get intimidated by modern tech.

column74: Painter / wage idea, Paint feedback on the tape, Automatic arm measurement, Spoken instructions and captions, Pause and rest breaks
column76: I'm 62 and honestly, I really liked the painter theme and getting that little pay slip at the end. It didn't feel like some silly kids game with cartoon characters. Made me feel like I was clocking in to do real work, and seeing what I earned actually made me want to finish the shift.
column77: A couple of times the brush stopped painting all of a sudden and restarted the stroke. Took me a minute to realize it was because I was leaning sideways in my chair. The red warning on screen popped up and vanished way too fast for me to catch it.
column78: Give a distinct chime or have the spoken voice tell me 'sit up straight' when my posture slips. At my age my eyes aren't quick enough to read tiny text warnings while I'm focusing on moving my arm.
column79: I worked in mail handling years back, so that postal sorter trade would be fantastic if you put it in next! Moving my left arm through the whole shift got the blood flowing nicely without tiring me out too much.
column87: Maybe put in a reminder telling us to take a quick rest if our shoulder starts creeping up toward our ears. When you're trying hard to finish the wall you don't even notice your shoulder hunching until it aches later that evening.

column74: Large text and high contrast, Spoken instructions and captions, Pause and rest breaks, Paint feedback on the tape
column76: I turned 65 in August and I've never touched a video game in my life, but this was surprisingly peaceful. The text was nice and big, colors were easy on the eyes, and following the masking tape made it very clear what to do without feeling overwhelmed.
column77: Holding my arm straight out for that 3 second check right at the start was pretty tough on my shoulder. And having the webcam pointed at me the whole time made me a little uneasy sitting alone in my room.
column78: Put a simple note right on the screen saying the camera isn't recording or sending video over the internet. That'd give plenty of peace of mind to folks my age who aren't tech savvy.
column79: The baker trade with kneading dough would be wonderful. I've baked bread for my family every Sunday for 40 years, and those motions would be great for stiff hands and wrists.
column87: Let people rest their elbow on the armrest or table during that first arm check. Holding the whole arm up in the air before you even start painting is a lot if your shoulder is already weak.
